Batch 5 manual enrichment — A Taxpayer v The Commissioners for HMRC

key_facts: The appellant moved to Ireland before receiving about £8m in dividends and claimed non-UK residence for 2015/16.
Under the statutory residence test she would be UK resident if present at the end of more than 45 days in the UK.
She argued six days in December 2015 and February 2016 did not count because she stayed to care for her twin sister's neglected children during an alcoholism crisis.
The FTT allowed her appeal; the UT reversed; the Court of Appeal restored the FTT decision.
enrichment.short_title: Exceptional circumstances day-counting in statutory residence test
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Upper Tribunal's decision reversing the First-tier Tribunal on Schedule 45 paragraph 22(4) exceptional circumstances.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; the First-tier Tribunal decision was restored.
enrichment.ratio: Paragraph 22(4) must be applied to the circumstances as a whole; compelling moral obligations to care for a close relative's minor children during a household crisis can constitute exceptional circumstances preventing departure, and whether circumstances are 'exceptional' is primarily a question of fact reviewable only on Edwards v Bairstow principles.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'prevented from leaving' in paragraph 22(4)
Whether moral obligations can form part of exceptional circumstances
Question of law vs fact for 'exceptional' assessment
Day-by-day application of paragraph 22(4)
linked_authorities: Edwards v Bairstow
Cozens v Brutus
Moyna v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions
R v Kelly (Edward)
Financial Conduct Authority v Arch Insurance (UK) Ltd

notes: First appellate consideration of the statutory residence test; analysis is detailed.

storyline.title: Sister's childcare crisis keeps six UK days out of residence count
storyline.summary: A taxpayer who relocated to Ireland before a large dividend relied on the statutory residence test's exceptional-circumstances rule for six days spent helping her alcoholic twin sister care for neglected children. HMRC denied the days; the Upper Tribunal agreed. The Court of Appeal restored the tribunal's fact-sensitive finding that the crisis was exceptional and prevented her leaving.

key_facts: Yukos shareholders obtained US $50bn+ Energy Charter Treaty awards against Russia and sought enforcement in England.
Russia challenged jurisdiction on state immunity grounds, disputing any written arbitration agreement.
The Hague Court of Appeal held Russia had agreed to arbitrate; Russia sought to re-argue the point in England.
Cockerill J held the Dutch decision created an issue estoppel; Russia appealed.
enrichment.short_title: Issue estoppel on state immunity arbitration exception
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal against a preliminary issue decision that Dutch court rulings estopped Russia from denying a section 9 State Immunity Act arbitration agreement.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Although the State Immunity Act 1978 comprehensively defines exceptions to immunity, it does not prescribe how they are proved; where a foreign court has finally decided that a state agreed in writing to arbitrate and ordinary issue-estoppel conditions are met (including section 31 recognition requirements), the English court may rely on that decision when applying the section 9 exception.
legal_issues: Whether issue estoppel applies to state immunity determinations
Interaction of State Immunity Act 1978 and foreign judgments
Requirements for transnational issue estoppel
Special circumstances exception
linked_authorities: Carl Zeiss Stiftung v Rayner & Keeler Ltd (No 2)
The Good Challenger
JH Rayner (Mincing Lane) Ltd v Department of Trade and Industry
Associated Electric & Gas Insurance Services Ltd v European Reinsurance Co of Zurich

records.notes: Batch 5 manual enrichment — Kristie Higgs v Farmor's School

key_facts: Kristie Higgs, a Christian pastoral administrator, was reported for Facebook posts opposing relationships education and gender ideology.
Farmor's School suspended and dismissed her for gross misconduct in January 2019 following a disciplinary process.
The employment tribunal dismissed direct discrimination and harassment claims; the EAT remitted the direct discrimination issue.
Underhill LJ allowed the appeal, substituting a finding that her dismissal was direct discrimination because of religion or belief.
enrichment.short_title: School dismissal for Facebook posts was belief discrimination
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Employment Appeal Tribunal's decision remitting whether dismissal was direct religion-or-belief discrimination.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on direct discrimination (substituted finding of success); appeal dismissed on remaining remitted issues.
enrichment.ratio: Where an employee is dismissed because of manifestations of a protected philosophical belief on social media, tribunals must identify the reason for dismissal and apply a justification analysis; here the school's concerns did not justify dismissing the employee for expressing beliefs protected after Forstater, and the dismissal was direct discrimination under section 13.
legal_issues: Direct discrimination because of religion or belief
Manifestation of protected beliefs on social media
Justification and proportionality under Equality Act 2010
Harassment and indirect discrimination remittal

records.notes: Batch 6 manual enrichment — Working on Wellbeing Ltd Trading as Optima Health v Secretary of State for Work and Pensions & Anor

key_facts: Optima Health bid for a DWP call-off contract under an existing framework for workplace health services.

key_facts: CD, a 17-year-old with complex needs, was subject to deprivation of liberty orders and an interim care order while living at home with 24-hour professional carers.

records.notes: Batch 6 manual enrichment — General Dynamics United Kingdom Limited v The State of Libya

key_facts: Libya contracted with GDUK in 2008 for a tactical communications system governed by Swiss law with ICC arbitration in Geneva.
An ICC award of over £16m was recognised in England; GDUK sought a charging order over Libyan property in London.

records.notes: Batch 2 manual enrichment — Amjad Ali Chaudhry v Secretary of State for the Home Department

key_facts: Mr Chaudhry was naturalised in 2005 but the Secretary of State later decided he had obtained citizenship by false representation relating to a passport in a deceased child's name.
The FTT allowed his appeal on Wednesbury review; the UT set aside that decision and restored deprivation, applying Ciceri and Chimi.
The Secretary of State changed her submissions on the proper FTT test during the proceedings.
The Court of Appeal held the FTT has a fact-finding role on fraud but public law review applies to causation and discretion.

enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Upper Tribunal on the proper approach to First-tier Tribunal appeals against deprivation under section 40(3) of the British Nationality Act 1981.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part; UT decision set aside; Chaudhry's appeal remitted to the FTT for rehearing before a different judge.

key_facts: M, an infant, lived with her mother while her father, a convicted sex offender, was excluded under section 38A.
Threshold was conceded; the dispute was whether the mother could protect M from future risk of sexual harm.
HHJ Bugeja made a care order placing M with paternal grandparents; the mother, father, guardian and grandparents opposed removal.

enrichment.short_title: Care order set aside for flawed risk assessment
enrichment.procedural_posture: Mother's appeal against final care order removing infant from her care to paternal grandparents.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; care order set aside and case remitted with interim care order.
enrichment.ratio: Before removing a securely attached infant from a parent's care, the court must conduct structured risk assessment identifying likelihood and timeframe of harm, available mitigation including shadow care plans and therapy, and a side-by-side welfare comparison of realistic options; failure to do so renders a care order disproportionate even where the father poses significant risk.

key_facts: Noel Clarke sued Guardian Newspapers over eight articles alleging serial abuse of women; meanings were determined at a preliminary trial.

statutes_considered.title: Council of Europe Convention against Trafficking in Human Beings

key_facts: Two related appeals concerned victims of trafficking (VLT and S) refused discretionary leave under version 10 of the DLP after positive conclusive grounds decisions.
The Upper Tribunal held transitional DLP provisions required KTT-cohort VOTs with outstanding asylum claims to be granted DL, and that a deportation carve-out was unlawful.
VLT had a deportation order; S was a foreign criminal also subject to deportation proceedings.
The Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State's appeals, holding the XY concession applied only to non-deportation KTT cohort members and S's article 14 cross-appeal failed.
enrichment.short_title: KTT cohort DL — deportation carve-out lawful; XY concession only for non-deportation VOTs

enrichment.outcome: Secretary of State's appeals allowed; S's article 14 cross-appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: DLP transitional provisions lawfully give most KTT-cohort VOTs the XY concession (deciding leave under pre-2022 Act policy as in KTT) but exclude those subject to deportation orders or proceedings, who are considered individually under the post-30 January 2023 VTS/VTSP scheme; that deportation carve-out is not an unlawful article 14 discrimination.

Whether KTT reasoning on ECAT compliance still governs interpretation of the DLP
Lawfulness of excluding deportation cases from the XY concession

key_facts: Ryanair withdrew discretionary staff travel from UK pilots who took BALPA strike action in September 2019.

records.notes: Batch 8 manual enrichment — Sandhu v Enterprise Rent-A-Car Ltd

key_facts: Ms Sandhu brought ET claims for discrimination, harassment and unfair dismissal against Enterprise Rent-A-Car.

records.notes: Batch 8 manual enrichment — XYZ v Disclosure and Barring Service

key_facts: A teacher (XYZ) was barred by the DBS from working with children after misconduct findings, following separate TRA disciplinary proceedings.
The TRA panel had exonerated him on some allegations, but the DBS and UT reached different factual conclusions on essentially the same evidence.
XYZ appealed, arguing res judicata and that the UT was bound by TRA fact-findings under paragraph 16 of Schedule 3.
The Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal, holding the DBS is not bound by TRA findings and is not an adjudicatory body.
enrichment.short_title: DBS barring — not bound by TRA fact-findings; res judicata inapplicable
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Upper Tribunal (Administrative Appeals Chamber) dismissing an appeal against a DBS decision to include a teacher on the children's barred list.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; barring decision upheld.
enrichment.ratio: The DBS is not an organ of the State exercising an adjudicatory function; disciplinary proceedings before the TRA and barring proceedings before the DBS have different purposes, so res judicata and Hunter principles do not bind the DBS or UT to TRA fact-findings, though those findings may be given such weight as is appropriate.
legal_issues: Whether paragraph 16 Schedule 3 SVGA 2006 creates issue estoppel from TRA proceedings
Application of res judicata and Hunter v Chief Constable to DBS barring
Weight to be given to TRA findings in DBS proceedings
Nature of DBS decision-making under SXM

records.notes: Batch 8 manual enrichment — Tesla Inc & Anor v InterDigital Patent Holdings, Inc & Ors

key_facts: Tesla sought declarations that Avanci and InterDigital must grant FRAND licences for UK SEPs relating to connected vehicles.
Mellor J granted permission to serve out on Avanci and InterDigital; Fancourt J refused representative licensing claims against InterDigital for the Avanci 5G Platform.
Arnold LJ allowed service-out appeals against Avanci and InterDigital but dismissed appeals on pool-licence and representative licensing claims.
The court held gateway 11 could apply to UK SEP licensing disputes but Tesla had no serious issue to be tried for a FRAND pool licence from Avanci.

enrichment.outcome: Mixed: appeals allowed on service out against Avanci and InterDigital; appeals dismissed on licensing/pool claims.
enrichment.ratio: A dispute over licensing UK SEPs on FRAND terms may fall within CPR PD 6B gateway 11, but Tesla has no serious issue to be tried for a declaration that Avanci must grant a pool licence where no such legal right exists; representative licensing claims against InterDigital for other platform members were rightly refused.

key_facts: Lonham insured Scotbeef's goods stored with D&S Storage; after a fire Scotbeef claimed under the policy.
Scotbeef succeeded on preliminary issues treating pre-contract information as representations under sections 3 and 9 rather than warranties under sections 10 and 11.
Lonham appealed, arguing the judge misclassified the information and failed to apply section 17 transparency requirements.

records.notes: Batch 2 manual enrichment — Sian Ivory v Welwyn Hatfield Borough Council

key_facts: Ms Ivory was found intentionally homeless after rent arrears eviction from Holliers Way; a third review rejected her mental breakdown explanation.
In September 2023 she made a fresh application supported by consultant psychiatrist Dr Okon-Rocha's report.
The council refused the application as based on the same facts; permission for judicial review was initially refused.

enrichment.ratio: A subsequent homelessness application must be accepted unless identical to the earlier application or any new matters are trivial or fanciful; significant new expert evidence supporting a previously rejected mental health allegation is a new fact, and authorities may not investigate accuracy at stage one per Rikha Begum and Minott.

key_facts: Mr Tipu, a Bangladeshi national, applied for an EEA residence card as an extended family member of his cousin Mr Ahmed.
The application was refused in November 2020; FTT and UT dismissed his appeals.
He could not show continuous dependency or household membership: a two-year gap while sponsor paid only Bangladesh university fees defeated the claim.

records.notes: Batch 2 manual enrichment — Aref Hussaini v Islington London Borough Council

key_facts: Mr Hussaini, an Afghan asylum seeker, attended the Baobab Centre in Islington three times weekly for PTSD therapy while housed in other boroughs.
Islington accepted he was homeless but referred his application to Haringey then Barking and Dagenham for lack of local connection.
He argued special circumstances under section 199(1)(d) because of therapeutic support and friendship with Dr Isayev near Islington.
The review officer found he did not need to live in Islington to access the Baobab Centre; the Court of Appeal dismissed the appeal.
enrichment.short_title: Local connection and therapeutic support in another borough
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from county court upholding review decision that homeless applicant had no local connection with Islington for referral purposes.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; referral decision upheld.
enrichment.ratio: A local connection by special circumstances does not require a threshold need to live in the district, but the review officer here did not impose such a test; absence of need to reside in Islington to access the Baobab Centre was a relevant factor and the decision was within the authority's margin of appreciation.
legal_issues: Whether review officer misdirected on need to live in Islington
Cumulative special circumstances including Baobab Centre, employment and friendship
Wednesbury reasonableness of no local connection finding

Eastleigh Borough Council v Betts [1983] 2 AC 613
Holmes-Moorhouse v Richmond upon Thames London Borough Council [2009] UKHL 7

records.notes: Batch 9 manual enrichment — Omar Elbanna v Tom Clark

key_facts: Mr Elbanna sued Mr Clark after a football pitch collision; causation was agreed and only breach of duty was tried before Sweeting J.
The parties agreed the negligence test from Czernuszka v King but the judge concluded at [33] that Mr Clark had been reckless.
Mr Clark appealed, arguing the recklessness finding was an unexplained error of law and sought to reopen factual grounds.
Whipple LJ granted permission on grounds 1, 2 and 5 (recklessness package) but refused grounds 3, 4, 6 and 7 as fact-finding challenges.
enrichment.short_title: Football injury appeal — permission on recklessness finding
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal from liability-only trial on agreed negligence test.
enrichment.outcome: Permission granted on grounds 1, 2 and 5; refused on grounds 3, 4, 6 and 7.
enrichment.ratio: Where the agreed test at trial was ordinary negligence but the judge's conclusion was expressed in terms of recklessness without explanation, there is an arguable error warranting full-court review; challenges to primary findings of fact are not permitted at the permission stage.
legal_issues: Whether Sweeting J erred by finding recklessness when negligence was the agreed test
Components of any recklessness standard if that was the judge's true finding
Scope of permission to appeal against unassailable fact findings

Condon v Basi

key_facts: Mr Tammina applied to extend Tier 2 leave relying on sponsor Ratna; compliance visit led to refusal in July 2017.

key_facts: Ethos Solutions operated a tax avoidance scheme channelling employee remuneration through a Jersey trust without PAYE/NIC.
HMRC assessed over £2.3m; the company entered CVL in 2012 without paying or appealing.
The liquidator sought s423 orders against 23 participants to recover tax that should have been deducted on trust payments (2009–2010).
Rajah J dismissed the claim; the Court of Appeal held preventing a tax liability arising is not a s423(3) purpose and upheld his rejection of the alternative fomite-to-HMRC case.
enrichment.short_title: Tax avoidance purpose not a section 423 prohibited purpose
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Rajah J's dismissal of liquidator's section 423 claims against Ethos scheme participants.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Entering transactions to ensure a tax liability does not accrue is not a section 423(3) purpose of prejudicing a creditor's claim; the words 'may make' require a present or future claim, not a hypothetical one prevented from arising; the alternative case that the company structured the scheme to impede HMRC if ineffective failed on the facts.

Distinction between tax mitigation and unacceptable tax avoidance in s423
Whether fomite/offshore trust structure showed purpose to impede HMRC recovery

key_facts: A single mother with two disabled sons was offered a final accommodation offer at Gretton Road; she refused and sought a suitability review under section 202(1)(h) only.
The review and county court appeal focused on suitability; the appellant later argued the authority should have decided any residual duty under section 190 after relief duty ended.
HHJ Saggerson dismissed the section 204 appeal; Nugee LJ granted permission on narrow grounds about scope of review.
The Court of Appeal held the statutory review/appeal route could not expand a suitability review into a wholesale duty assessment; appeal dismissed.
enrichment.short_title: Suitability review cannot expand into duty-scope appeal
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from county court dismissal of section 204 challenge to Haringey's June 2023 suitability review decision.

Scope of Temur and Ravichandran on combined reviews

key_facts: F4 was deprived of British citizenship while detained in Syria; she sought SIAC's extension of the 28-day appeal time limit under rule 8(5).

records.notes: Batch 10 manual enrichment — Expert Tooling and Automation Limited v Engie Power Limited

key_facts: Expert Tooling used broker Utilitywise to negotiate electricity contracts with Engie; UW received commission added to unit price with partial disclosure only.
Tooling claimed UW breached fiduciary duties and Engie procured the breach and received commissions as money had and received.
The judge found UW breached fiduciary duty but Tooling had given informed consent and Engie was not dishonest; claims against Engie dismissed.
The Court of Appeal allowed appeal on informed consent (grounds 2–4) but upheld dismissal on dishonesty, money had and received, and limitation (grounds 5–7).
enrichment.short_title: Half-secret energy broker commission and accessory liability
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from trial judgment dismissing Tooling's claims against Engie for procuring UW's breach of fiduciary duty and restitution of commissions.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part on grounds 2–4 (no informed consent to commissions); dismissed on grounds 5–7 (dishonesty required for accessory liability; no MHR claim; limitation).
enrichment.ratio: Partial disclosure of commission does not establish informed consent where material matters including amount and funding mechanism were not disclosed; vulnerability is not a substitute for disclosure; accessory liability for procuring breach of fiduciary duty requires dishonesty (Royal Brunei); paying commission to an agent without principal's informed consent is not recoverable as money had and received from the payer.
legal_issues: Scope of fiduciary duty vs informed consent
Material non-disclosure in half-secret commission cases
Dishonesty as element of accessory liability
Money had and received vs equitable compensation
Limitation and deliberate concealment

Royal Brunei Airlines v Tan
Bristol & West Building Society v Mothew
Hospital Products Ltd v United States Surgical Corporation

records.notes: Batch 10 manual enrichment — The Commissioners for HMRC v Innovative Bites Limited

key_facts: Innovative Bites sold 'Mega Marshmallows' marketed for roasting over campfires; packaging showed roasting, s'mores, and snacking.
The FTT zero-rated the product as food; the UT dismissed HMRC's appeal; HMRC appealed to the Court of Appeal.
The issue was whether Mega Marshmallows are confectionery under Note (5) as 'sweetened prepared food normally eaten with the fingers'.
The Court allowed HMRC's appeal and remitted to the FTT for factual findings on normal mode of consumption, with potential oral evidence.
enrichment.short_title: Mega Marshmallows VAT confectionery classification
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Upper Tribunal dismissing HMRC's challenge to zero-rating of Mega Marshmallows.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; remitted to FTT to determine whether product is normally eaten with the fingers within Note (5).
enrichment.ratio: Note (5) to Group 1 of Schedule 8 is a non-exhaustive deeming provision; if a product falls within its terms (including sweetened prepared food normally eaten with the fingers) it is standard-rated confectionery; the question is one of fact requiring assessment of how the product is normally consumed, not merely how it can be consumed; marketing and packaging are relevant but not determinative.
legal_issues: Construction of Note (5) confectionery deeming provision
Distinction between possible and normal modes of consumption
Role of packaging and marketing in VAT classification
Whether FTT/UT erred on burden and evidence

records.notes: Batch 3 manual enrichment — D8 v Secretary of State for the Home Department

statutes_considered.title: 1951 Geneva Convention relating to the Status of Refugees

key_facts: D8, an Iranian Kurdish national, was granted refugee status in 2017 but the Secretary of State revoked it in 2020 on national security grounds relating to Islamist support.
SIAC held revocation unlawful because the Secretary of State had not balanced national security risk against alternative measures and treated revocation as a measure of last resort.
D8 cannot be returned to Iran because of Article 2 and 3 risks; the Secretary of State accepts some form of leave must be granted regardless of the appeal outcome.
The Court of Appeal allowed the Secretary of State's appeal, holding no further balancing exercise is required once a refugee is reasonably regarded as a danger to national security.
enrichment.short_title: Refugee revocation — no last-resort balancing once national security danger found
enrichment.procedural_posture: Secretary of State's appeal from SIAC's OPEN judgment quashing revocation of refugee status and refusal of a further asylum claim on national security grounds.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; SIAC's decision set aside on the balancing-exercise point.
enrichment.ratio: Once the Secretary of State lawfully concludes that a refugee is a danger to national security, she is not required to balance that danger against the cost or practicability of surveillance or other risk-reduction measures before revoking refugee status; Article 33(2) and equivalent domestic provisions contain their own balance and section 34 ATCS 2001 excludes a further proportionality exercise of the kind SIAC undertook.
legal_issues: Whether revocation of refugee status requires a last-resort balancing exercise
Interpretation of CJEU decision in T v Land Baden-Wurttemberg as retained EU case law
Weight of UNHCR guidance on proportionality under Article 33(2)
Relationship between Refugee Convention, Qualification Directive, and Immigration Rules

records.notes: Batch 10 manual enrichment — F and B (Fact-Finding: Gonorrhoea)

key_facts: Six-year-old F was diagnosed with gonorrhoea in June 2023 during care proceedings; the local authority alleged sexual abuse by the mother or maternal uncle X.
Experts Dr Ghaly and Dr Rothburn said gonorrhoea in a prepubertal child is strongly suggestive of sexual abuse; fomite transmission is rare and theoretical.
HHJ Greensmith found fomite transmission facilitated by X who knew he was contagious, rejecting sexual abuse on the balance of probabilities.
The Court of Appeal allowed the appeal, holding the judge misapplied expert evidence and flawed his Lucas lie analysis; fact-finding remitted to another judge.
enrichment.short_title: Gonorrhoea fact-finding and misapplication of expert evidence
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from reserved fact-finding judgment in care proceedings rejecting sexual abuse and finding fomite transmission.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; fact-finding hearing remitted before another judge.
enrichment.ratio: Where expert evidence states gonorrhoea in a young child is strongly suggestive of sexual abuse and fomite transmission is no more than a rare theoretical possibility, a judge errs by treating non-exclusion of fomite transmission as sufficient to reject abuse on the balance of probabilities; excessive weight on 'not impossible' fomite transfer is inconsistent with the medical evidence; flawed application of Lucas principles to X's lies also warrants intervention.
legal_issues: Weight to be given to expert medical evidence on mode of transmission
Standard of proof in fact-finding on sexual abuse
Fomite vs sexual transmission of gonorrhoea
Lucas direction on lies told by X
Appellate intervention in evaluative fact-finding

key_facts: Merck Global and Merck US (MSD) have a long-running dispute over use of the 'Merck' name under a 2016 coexistence agreement and 2020 Final Order.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Robert Ian Winsor v Timothy Hull Pattinson

key_facts: Mr Winsor, brother-in-law of District Judge Pattinson, sent 17 emails breaching a Steyn J harassment injunction between March and May 2024 alleging fraud over a £130,000 bankruptcy recovery.
Linden J found contempt proved at trial in September 2024 and imposed a suspended four-month committal in November 2024; Bean LJ refused permission to challenge the liability finding.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Plymouth Community Homes Limited v Crisplane Limited

key_facts: Two right-to-buy flats at Rothesay Gardens, Plymouth, had leases excluding roof repairs from the lessee's 50% service charge contribution.
Plymouth Community Homes replaced ageing roofs in 2018; Crisplane denied liability for roughly £7,965.60 per flat.
The Upper Tribunal allowed Crisplane's appeal; separate construction arguments applied to flats 96 and 146.
The Court of Appeal agreed with the UT: statutory implied repairing covenants do not automatically create a matching payment obligation.
enrichment.short_title: Right-to-buy lease roof repairs and service charge
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Upper Tribunal decision allowing lessee's appeal against service charge liability for roof works.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: Under right-to-buy leases, a lessee's obligation to contribute half of costs under Schedule 4 is tied to express landlord covenants in Schedule 4, not to the landlord's separate statutory implied covenant to repair the roof; excluding the roof from paragraph 5 limits the lessee's contribution even though the landlord remains obliged to repair; general First Schedule 'shelter' rights do not override an express roof exclusion.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Hammad Tazeem, R (on the application of) v Secretary of State for the Home Department

key_facts: Pakistani student Mr Tazeem arrived at Heathrow in September 2022; Border Force cancelled his leave after interviews raised doubts about his English proficiency and test authenticity.
The cancellation decision was procedurally unfair under Balajigari, but that finding was not appealed by the SSHD.
The deputy judge held detention pending examination was lawful; the Court of Appeal held post-decision detention from about 02:32 on 10 September was unlawful.
Damages of £4,500 were assessed for 11–12 hours of unlawful detention at the airport.
enrichment.short_title: Unlawful detention after unfair leave cancellation
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from deputy High Court judge's decision that immigration detention at Heathrow was lawful.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; unlawful detention for 11–12 hours declared; damages assessed at £4,500.
enrichment.ratio: Detention pending examination under paragraph 16 of Schedule 2 is lawful until a decision to cancel leave is made; once that decision is made and the examination ends, continued detention requires separate lawful justification; an unlawful cancellation decision taints subsequent detention for removal; a 'period of grace' after Hardial Singh does not apply where the detainee had valid leave treated as a nullity and posed no public safety risk.
legal_issues: Whether unlawful cancellation decision retrospectively taints initial detention
When paragraph 16 detention ends after examination concludes
Applicability of Hardial Singh grace period principles
Quantum for short airport detention

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Stefanos Neophytou, R (on the application of) v The Governor of HMP Berwyn & Anor

key_facts: Mr Neophytou serves a 10-year default term for non-payment of a £3.17m confiscation order after 2014 kidnap trauma.
He applied for early release on compassionate grounds citing complex PTSD worsened by imprisonment; expert reports said therapy could not occur in prison.
Governor Keller refused to refer the health-based ERCG application to PPCS, applying paragraph 4.17 criteria and policy paragraph 1.4(c).
The Court of Appeal held the governor could only refuse if it was clear paragraph 4.17 criteria were not met and must submit borderline cases to PPCS.

enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from judicial review dismissal of challenge to prison governor's refusal to submit ERCG application to PPCS.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; governor's refusal quashed; fresh governor decision required.
enrichment.ratio: For ERCG applications based on health under paragraph 4.21 of the Policy, the governor has delegated authority to refuse only where it is clear the paragraph 4.17 criteria are not met; paragraph 1.4(c) does not authorise refusal on health grounds; exacerbation of PTSD in custody may satisfy paragraph 4.17 even where condition pre-dated activation of the default term; the governor cannot pre-empt the Secretary of State's ultimate ERCG decision.

Application of paragraph 1.4(c) to default-term prisoners
Whether paragraph 4.17 requires 'exceptional' circumstances at governor stage
Section 31(2A) where outcome would differ if application referred

key_facts: Jamaican national Mr Geddes was convicted of wounding with intent in 2007; deportation decision made in 2014.
He exhausted FTT, UT, and Court of Appeal routes, then filed a Supreme Court permission application in 2017.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Dhasarathan Seerangan v Secretary of State for the Home Department

key_facts: Indian national Mr Seerangan overstayed after his student visa expired in January 2022 and requested a Covid exceptional assurance in November 2022.
UKVI refused a full exceptional assurance but granted a two-week short-term assurance until 30 November 2022.
He applied for skilled worker leave on 29 November 2022; the application was refused because he was an overstayer.
The Court of Appeal held the EA Policy protected only regularised overstayers and the UKVI letter did not create a clear legitimate expectation to disregard overstaying.
enrichment.short_title: Covid exceptional assurance and overstayer skilled worker claim
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission from Upper Tribunal dismissal of judicial review of skilled worker refusal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: The Covid exceptional assurance policy distinguished regularised overstayers (who applied before visa expiry and renewed assurances) from unregularised overstayers; a short-term assurance given when travel restrictions no longer applied did not clearly and unambiguously undertake that the recipient would not be treated as an overstayer for an in-country skilled worker application; paragraph 13 of the UKVI letter could not sensibly create such an expectation in those circumstances.
legal_issues: Construction of the EA Policy sections A, B, and C
Whether unregularised overstayers could obtain belated protection
Legitimate expectation and Finucane standard
Whether UKVI letter paragraph 13 was a clear undertaking

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Muhammad Arshad v Secretary of State for The Home Department

key_facts: Pakistani overstayer Mr Arshad lived with his sister and helped care for her three children for over six years.
The FTT allowed his 2020 human rights appeal under GEN3.2, finding removal would have unjustifiably harsh consequences for the children.
The UT held the FTT erred by failing to treat family life formed during unlawful presence as a mandatory relevant consideration requiring little weight.
The Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Arshad's appeal, agreeing precariousness must be weighed in the proportionality balance.
enrichment.short_title: Article 8 uncle claim and precarious family life
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Upper Tribunal decision setting aside FTT allowance of human rights appeal and remaking decision to dismiss.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.

Whether FTT applied GEN3.2 correctly
Weight of delay in enforcement (EB Kosovo)
Distinction between uncle relationship and parental family life

key_facts: Mrs Davies lodged an EAT appeal on the last day of the 42-day limit but omitted the ET judgment from her submission.
The missing judgment was supplied on 22 March 2022, about 140 days late; the Registrar and HHJ Tucker refused an extension.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — SA v The Secretary of State for The Home Department

key_facts: Protected party SA obtained refugee status in 2009 on a false Saudi identity; SSHD revoked status in 2021 after discovering Yemeni nationality and forged documents.
The FTT dismissed the section 84(3)(a) appeal but allowed section 84(3)(b), granting humanitarian protection for Yemen despite SA denying Yemeni nationality.
The UT identified a jurisdictional error: a revocation appeal under section 84(3)(b) must focus on the country of origin in the original claim (Saudi Arabia), not Yemen.
The Court of Appeal agreed on merits but held the UT should have invited submissions on the point; prejudice was cured on appeal.
enrichment.short_title: Revocation appeal jurisdiction and procedural fairness
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from Upper Tribunal decision setting aside FTT allowance of humanitarian protection on revocation appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; UT decision upheld; procedural irregularity cured on appeal.
enrichment.ratio: On an appeal under section 84(3)(c) against revocation of refugee status, section 84(3)(b) requires assessment of whether revocation breaches obligations relating to persons eligible for humanitarian protection by reference to the country of origin in the original protection claim; the FtT had no jurisdiction to grant humanitarian protection based on Yemen when the claimant denied Yemeni nationality and never claimed protection there; a tribunal may raise a jurisdictional point of its own motion but should invite submissions before deciding.
legal_issues: Scope of section 84(3)(b) on revocation appeals
Country of origin for humanitarian protection assessment
Robinson obviousness and procedural fairness
Whether to remit for further hearing after UT procedural error

key_facts: Mr Chowdhury's leave to remain was refused because a 2013 TOEIC certificate was deemed fraudulently obtained at Eden College.

records.notes: Batch 11 manual enrichment — Matthew Carter v The Chief Constable of Essex Police

key_facts: Mr Carter was arrested in December 2017 after a pub assault allegation and became agitated at Southend Police Station.
PS Bailey ordered forcible removal of his clothing for an anti-self-harm suit after he bit an officer's glove during restraint.
The recorder found the strip in Cell 28 unlawful; the High Court held section 54(4)(a) requires only genuine belief, not reasonable belief.
The Court of Appeal dismissed grounds 1–3, holding belief need not be reasonable; force in Cell 28 was necessary; damages award would have been too high.
enrichment.short_title: PACE section 54(4)(a) belief and strip in custody
enrichment.procedural_posture: Second appeal from High Court reversal of recorder's findings on lawfulness of forcible clothing removal in police custody.

enrichment.ratio: Section 54(4)(a) PACE requires the custody officer actually to hold the relevant belief that clothes may be used to cause physical injury; it does not require that belief to be reasonable, though unreasonableness may undermine proof of actual belief; Code C Annex A paragraph 11 applies only in spirit to safety removals; appellate court may interfere where recorder misapplied context including positional asphyxia risk and venial use-of-force analysis.

Application of PD and Annex A to anti-self-harm clothing removals

statutes_considered.title: Administration Charges (Summary of Rights and Obligations) (England) Regulations 2007

key_facts: RTM company claimed £616.60 service charge arrears, £3,240 variable administration charges and FTT costs from leaseholder Mr Davies.

records.notes: Batch 13 manual enrichment — Darren White v Michael Alder & Anor

key_facts: Neighbours disputed the boundary between Willow Cottage and The Old Stores after predecessors orally agreed its location in 2005.
District Judge Mills found the boundary demarcation agreement binding on successors; HHJ Duddridge dismissed most grounds but granted permission on successor binding.

enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from HHJ Duddridge's refusal of permission on whether a boundary agreement binds successors without knowledge.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed.
enrichment.ratio: A boundary demarcation agreement that merely clarifies an uncertain boundary has proprietary effect, defines the extent of the parcels conveyed, and binds successors in title without the need for knowledge; Gibson v New did not alter Neilson v Poole and the Court of Appeal authorities endorsing it.

records.notes: Batch 13 manual enrichment — YVR, R (on the application of) v Birmingham City Council

key_facts: A severely disabled young man challenged Birmingham's adult social care charging policy after R (SH) v Norfolk identified discriminatory treatment of those unable to work.
Birmingham reviewed its policy post-Norfolk but largely retained maximum statutory charges amid severe financial crisis.
Mrs Justice Collins Rice upheld the policy as justified; the appeal focused on whether the PSED required Cabinet-level consideration.
The Court of Appeal held officers who lawfully took the decision were the relevant decision-makers for section 149 purposes.
enrichment.short_title: PSED and delegated adult social care charging decisions
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from refusal of permission to judicial review of Birmingham's 2023 charging policy.

Whether Cabinet had to consider section 149 before maintaining maximum charges
Whether officers gathered sufficient evidence of impact on severely disabled people

key_facts: Following Sara Sharif's murder, journalists sought disclosure of historic family proceedings and challenged anonymisation of three circuit judges in a reporting restrictions order.

key_facts: A severely disabled 12-year-old received NHS continuing care commissioned by North Central London ICB through Enviva; the ICB terminated Enviva on 9 July 2024 and sought Nursing Direct from 10 July 2024.

Parents privately funded Enviva and Practical Staffing at about £10,000 per week after refusing Nursing Direct; MacDonald J granted JR on missing updated Section G health care plan but dismissed irrational termination and restitution grounds.

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Management Procedure) (England) Order 2015

key_facts: Isle of Wight Council granted planning permission on 4 August 2023 for 473 homes at Ryde subject to a section 106 agreement including £406,359 highway contributions.
The proposed and final section 106 agreement was not placed on the planning register as required by article 40(3)(b) DMPO 2015.
Greenfields (IOW) Ltd judicially reviewed the grant; HHJ Jarman KC dismissed most grounds but refused permission on the register breach.
The Court of Appeal allowed ground 1, holding the August 2023 permission invalid, and dismissed other grounds.

legal_issues: Invalidity consequences of article 40(3)(b) DMPO breach
Application of section 31(2A) where highway contribution amount was unpublished
Material considerations and Pennyfeathers site allocation

Batch 3 manual enrichment — FS Capital Limited  & Ors v Alan Adams & Ors

key_facts: FS Capital bought loan assets worth hundreds of millions from Jersey trusts controlled by Emblin, Reid and O'Shea for nominal consideration.
Johnson J held the disposal was for an improper purpose, void in equity, and FS Capital was not a bona fide purchaser for value without notice.
Appellants argued Jersey law treated improper exercise of power as voidable not void; experts disagreed on unsettled Jersey law.
The Court of Appeal dismissed appeals, holding Jersey follows English law that improper purpose exercises are void, including under Cloutte v Storey.

enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeals from High Court decision that FS Capital's purchase of Jersey trust loan assets was void and FS Capital must reconstitute the trusts.

legal_issues: Whether improper exercise of trustee power is void or voidable under Jersey law
Accessory liability of Pinotage for retirement facilitating breach
Bona fide purchaser for value without notice

records.notes: Batch 4 manual enrichment — Airwave Solutions Limited & Ors v Competition and Markets Authority & Anor

key_facts: Motorola's Airwave Solutions held a monopoly on emergency-services radio after the 2000 PFI fixed term expired and ESN replacement was delayed.
The CMA found an adverse effect on competition and imposed a charge control capping revenue by about £1.2 billion over the extension period.
The CAT upheld the decision on judicial review; Motorola sought permission to appeal on dynamic competition and asset valuation grounds.
The Court of Appeal refused permission, holding the CAT was entitled to find ESN did not constrain pricing and asset transfer defects were part of the AEC analysis.
enrichment.short_title: Airwave PFI extension pricing and CMA charge control upheld
enrichment.procedural_posture: Deferred permission-to-appeal application with immediate substantive hearing against the Competition Appeal Tribunal's refusal of Motorola's judicial review of the CMA market investigation.
enrichment.outcome: Permission to appeal refused on both grounds.
enrichment.ratio: Long-term dynamic competition from the delayed ESN project did not necessarily constrain Motorola's post-expiry monopoly pricing; the CMA's zero asset valuation for the extension period and criticism of PFI asset-transfer provisions were rational and internally consistent, not irrational or based on a misreading that those provisions were excluded from the AEC finding.
legal_issues: Whether ESN entry constituted a material competitive constraint in the CMA's section 4 assessment
Whether asset transfer provisions and zero valuation for amortised PFI assets were irrational
Standard of review of economic judgments by the CAT and CMA
linked_authorities: Société Coopérative de Production SeaFrance SA v CMA
Cerelia Group Holding SAS v CMA
Office of Fair Trading v IBA Healthcare Ltd

key_facts: Private children proceedings over three daughters involved repeated contested hearings maintaining broadly equal shared care since 2019.
In November 2023 the mother applied to vary arrangements; at a DRA Deputy District Judge O'Leary dismissed the application without a section 7 report and made a three-year section 91(14) order.

statutes_considered.title: Tribunal Procedure (First-tier Tribunal) (Immigration and Asylum Chamber) Rules 2014

key_facts: Ferdous Alam Khan, a Bangladeshi national, appealed against refusal of indefinite leave to remain relying on very significant obstacles to integration and Article 8.
The First-tier Tribunal dismissed his appeal on 5 March 2024 without expressly recording that he was a vulnerable witness under Joint Presidential Guidance Note No 2 of 2010.
The Upper Tribunal dismissed his appeal on 30 October 2024, holding any failure to follow the Guidance Note did not render the FTT decision procedurally unfair.
The Court of Appeal dismissed Mr Khan's sole ground, holding the Guidance Note gives guidance on fair participation rather than imposing free-standing legal obligations.
enrichment.short_title: Vulnerable witness guidance not a free-standing legal duty in FTT
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from the Upper Tribunal on whether the First-tier Tribunal erred by failing to follow Joint Presidential Guidance Note No 2 of 2010 on vulnerable witnesses.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; Upper Tribunal decision upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Joint Presidential Guidance Note No 2 of 2010 is guidance to assist fair and just participation in tribunal proceedings, not a set of free-standing legal obligations; failure to record vulnerability or follow paragraph 15 does not necessarily amount to procedural unfairness where the appellant was represented by leading counsel, gave effective evidence, and no prejudice is shown.

Whether failure to record vulnerability under paragraph 15 is always a material error of law
Relationship between AM (Afghanistan) and mandatory compliance with tribunal guidance
Whether procedural unfairness must be shown beyond bare non-compliance with guidance

key_facts: Kamran Safi, an Afghan national trafficked as a child, was convicted of aggravated burglary and sentenced to six years six months.

key_facts: WH Holding (West Ham) disputed a £3.6m Stadium Premium Amount claimed by London Stadium LLP (E20) after a 2021 share transaction.

key_facts: Two children aged 13 and 11 were subject to a Hague Convention return order to the United States made in 2024.
In [2025] EWCA Civ 1426 the Court of Appeal stayed return because suitable protective measures were not yet in place and adjourned the appeal.
On 13 January 2026 the father applied to withdraw his Hague Convention summons, stating he could no longer fight after years without contact since June 2021.
The children's representatives agreed to withdraw their appeal; the court set aside the return orders by consent without determining the merits.
enrichment.short_title: Father withdraws Hague return; return order set aside by consent
enrichment.procedural_posture: Disposal judgment following the Court of Appeal's main judgment in [2025] EWCA Civ 1426, recording consent orders on the children's Hague appeal.
enrichment.outcome: Father's application to withdraw the Hague Convention summons granted; children's appeal withdrawn; return orders of November 2024 and July 2025 set aside by consent under CPR PD52A 6.4.
enrichment.ratio: Where a Hague return appeal has been adjourned and the left-behind parent withdraws the underlying Convention application, the court may set aside the return order by consent without determining the merits, provided there are good and sufficient reasons; the court recorded that the original return decision remained proper in principle.
legal_issues: Disposal of a stayed Hague Convention appeal after withdrawal of the underlying summons
Setting aside a return order by consent under CPR PD52A 6.4
Whether the court should allow the children's appeal on the merits after the father's withdrawal
linked_authorities: [2025] EWCA Civ 1426

key_facts: Allen generated at least £30,000 from stolen-bicycle dealing October 2014–October 2015 while receiving income-related ESA until 5 April 2016.

key_facts: Zaha Hadid Limited licensed ZAHA HADID trade marks from Dame Zaha Hadid, now owned by the Zaha Hadid Foundation.
The 2013 licence continues indefinitely but only the licensor may terminate on three months' notice; royalty is 6% of net income.
Adam Johnson J held no implied right for the licensee to terminate on reasonable notice and rejected restraint of trade.

enrichment.short_title: Indefinite trade mark licence terminable on reasonable notice

enrichment.ratio: Where a trade mark licence states it shall 'continue indefinitely, unless terminated earlier in accordance with' clauses granting termination rights only to the licensor, the natural construction is indefinite duration for both parties, implying a power for either party to terminate on reasonable notice following Winter Garden Theatre line of authority; perpetual lock-in is commercially implausible.

key_facts: Tower Hamlets implemented a 14-closure LTN in Bethnal Green January 2020–March 2022; new Mayor revoked it 20 September 2023 after consultation, retaining one closure.
Resident Oliver Hawes judicially reviewed revocation; Fordham J dismissed the claim 17 December 2024.
Court of Appeal allowed appeal on issue 1 only — revocation breached s.151(1)(a) duty to implement the Local Implementation Plan.
enrichment.short_title: LTN revocation breached LIP implementation duty
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review appeal against dismissal of challenge to Mayor's decision revoking Bethnal Green LTN.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on issue 1 (s.151 GLAA 1999); issues 2 and 3 rejected; quashing order indicated for revocation decision.
enrichment.ratio: Section 151(1)(a) GLAA 1999 requires a London borough to implement proposals in its Local Implementation Plan according to the timetable; revoking an implemented LTN that formed part of the LIP without amending the plan breaches that duty — the question is whether proposals have been implemented, not whether traffic outcomes match forecasts.
legal_issues: Breach of s.151(1)(a) duty to implement LIP proposals
Whether Mayor failed to have regard to LIP as material consideration
Fairness of consultation on Option 3 not adopted
Role of TfL as interested party
linked_authorities: R (Hammersmith) v Mayor of London [2015] EWHC 856
R (Moseley) v Haringey LBC [2014] UKSC 56

key_facts: PC Lino Di Maria faced rape and other allegations; misconduct investigations found no case to answer but vetting was withdrawn September 2023.
Lang J allowed judicial review holding vetting could not find reasonable suspicion of same conduct after acquittal/no case to answer absent exceptional circumstances.
Court of Appeal allowed Commissioner appeal on Ground 3 only — reasonable suspicion is a lower threshold than misconduct standard of proof.
enrichment.short_title: Police vetting: reasonable suspicion after no case to answer
enrichment.procedural_posture: Commissioner appeal with permission on Ground 3 only (other grounds withdrawn after 2025 Regulations); challenge to Lang J vetting Code interpretation.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed on Ground 3; Lang J erred — vetting may find reasonable grounds to suspect conduct occurred despite earlier no case to answer finding.
enrichment.ratio: The vetting test of reasonable grounds to suspect is a lower threshold than the balance of probabilities applied in misconduct proceedings; a finding of no case to answer or that misconduct is not proved does not preclude a vetting review from concluding there are reasonable grounds to suspect the same conduct unless exceptional circumstances exist — and the Judge wrongly equated the two standards.
legal_issues: Interaction between Conduct Regulations and College of Policing Vetting Code
Whether vetting may revisit conduct cleared in misconduct process
Meaning of reasonable grounds to suspect vs balance of probabilities
Jurisdiction and discretion to hear appeal after 2025 Regulations
linked_authorities: Mallett v McMonagle [1970] AC 166
Shaaban bin Hussein v Chong Fook Kam [1970] AC 942
R (Secretary of State) v Reilly

key_facts: FS Commercial submitted VAT return 08/18; HMRC requested invoices over £1k input tax including Verity-related payments.
Company failed to produce Verity invoices; HMRC refused input tax deduction; FTT and UT held tribunal jurisdiction was supervisory only.

Court of Appeal dismissed appeal; HMRC's refusal was an exercise of discretion under regulation 29(2) for lack of invoices or sufficient alternative evidence, so the FTT's jurisdiction was supervisory only.
enrichment.short_title: VAT input tax refusal under Reg 29(2) — supervisory FTT jurisdiction
enrichment.procedural_posture: Taxpayer appeal against Upper Tribunal decision that the FTT's jurisdiction over HMRC's regulation 29(2) refusal of input tax was supervisory rather than fully appellate.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; where HMRC refuses input tax by exercising regulation 29(2) because compliant invoices or sufficient alternative evidence were not produced in time, the FTT reviews that discretion on supervisory principles and cannot rehear the case with withheld invoices.
enrichment.ratio: When HMRC refuses to allow input tax deduction by exercising its discretion under regulation 29(2) because the taxable person has not produced compliant invoices or sufficient alternative evidence before the decision, the FTT's jurisdiction is supervisory only; it cannot conduct a full rehearing admitting documents that should have been supplied to HMRC before the decision was made.
legal_issues: Character of HMRC decision refusing input tax deduction
Whether Reg 29(2) discretion was exercised
Supervisory vs appellate FTT jurisdiction
Effect of Pegasus Birds on VAT assessments
linked_authorities: Pegasus Birds Ltd v Customs and Excise [2004] EWCA Civ 1015
R (O) v Hammersmith LBC
Commissioners v Aken [1990] 1 WLR 1374
